items.title: Things to know
How to care for plants purchased from a plant nursery?

items.text: To care for new nursery plants, immediately inspect them for pests, clean the leaves, and water thoroughly if the soil is dry. Allow plants 24–48 hours to adjust in a shaded, sheltered spot before planting or repotting to prevent shock. Keep soil consistently moist initially, avoid immediate heavy fertilization, and monitor daily.
This video shows what to do with a new plant when you bring it home:

items.title: Steps for New Nursery Plants:
items.text: Quarantine and Inspect: Isolate new plants from existing ones for a few weeks to prevent the spread of hidden pests. Check for insects or damage on leaves and in the soil. Acclimation: Let the plant rest in a bright, sheltered, but shady location for 1–2 days, especially if it has been transported in harsh weather. Watering: Immediately check the soil moisture. Water until it drains from the bottom of the pot. If the soil is very dry, place the pot in a tray of water for about an hour. Repotting or Planting: Plant in the ground as soon as possible, as it is easier to keep them alive there than in pots. If potting, wait about a week before moving it to a larger container to reduce stress. Clean and Prune: Remove any dead, yellow, or damaged leaves to encourage new growth. Light and Placement: Ensure the plant is placed in a spot that matches its specific light requirements (e.g., full sun vs. shade). Fertilizing: Avoid heavy fertilizing immediately after planting, as young roots are sensitive.

items.title: Key Benefits of Buying from a Plant Nursery
items.text: Superior Plant Health & Quality: Plants are generally better maintained, with stronger root systems and no signs of pests or neglect, as staff focus on specialized care. Locally Adapted & Native Species: Nurseries stock plants suited for your regional climate and soil, making them easier to maintain and more likely to thrive. Expert Knowledge and Support: Staff are typically knowledgeable gardeners who offer tailored advice on soil, watering, plant selection, and pest management. Diverse, Unique Inventory: Nurseries often provide a wider variety of plants, including rare specimens and seasonal offerings not found in mass retailers. Sustainable Practices & Freshness: Locally grown plants are often grown on-site or sourced locally, reducing transportation emissions and ensuring the plants are not stressed from long-distance shipping.

items.title: What are the environmental impacts of plant nurseries?

Plant nurseries have significant environmental impacts, primarily through nutrient runoff (nitrogen and phosphorus) that causes water eutrophication, contamination from pesticides, and heavy plastic waste from pots. They also contribute to greenhouse gas emissions and the spread of invasive species. Key issues include:
items.text: Water Pollution & Usage: High use of fertilizers and pesticides leads to contamination of groundwater and surface water. Container production requires extensive watering, and runoff can carry pollutants into local waterways. Plastic Pollution: Nurseries generate significant waste through non-recyclable or single-use plastic pots and containers, which are often not recycled. Invasive Species Spread: Nurseries can unintentionally propagate invasive plants that threaten local ecosystems. Pesticide Residues: Pesticides, including neonicotinoids, are often used, which can leave toxic residues harmful to pollinators, even on plants sold as "pollinator-friendly". Carbon Footprint: Container-grown plants have a higher carbon footprint than in-field production due to the energy-intensive production of plastic pots and growing media, with emissions ranging from 26.1 to 34.7 Mg CO2eq ha⁻¹ year⁻¹.

items.title: What is the history of plant nurseries?

items.text: Plant nurseries evolved from 17th-century colonial seedling efforts into a robust 18th-century commercial industry, pioneered by the 1737 Linnaean Botanic Garden and Nurseries in New York. Nurseries grew from supplying fruit trees and regional seeds to specializing in ornamental, exotic plants, and reforestation, expanding rapidly through catalogue sales and the 20th-century development of retail garden centers.

items.title: Key Historical Developments
items.text: 18th Century Roots: Robert Prince opened the first commercial nursery in the US in 1737 (Flushing, NY), supplying fruits and ornamental plants. 19th Century Expansion: Nurseries grew with specialized markets (roses, bulbs) and increased demand for varied landscapes, spurred by figures like Johnny Appleseed distributing seeds. 20th Century Industrialization: The 1915 Panama International Exposition displayed the nursery industry's commercial scale. State-run nurseries began in the early 1900s to support reforestation, such as in California and New York. Modernization: Mid-20th century saw the shift toward retail garden centers offering plants, tools, and supplies, further enhanced by the "Green Revolution" focusing on home gardening.

items.title: Usage Examples in History
items.text: Early American Horticulture: The Prince Nursery was used by colonial residents to acquire new, unique, and foreign plant species. Economic Independence: Post-Revolutionary, nurseries were vital for developing native species and creating a self-sufficient US agricultural industry. Reforestation & Conservation: In the 1900s, state nurseries were established to distribute cheap seedlings to reforest areas and restore private timber lands. Landscaping & Beautification: Nurseries supplied, designed, and planted trees for public highways and large expositions like the 1939-40 World's Fair. Research & Plant Breeding: Nurseries were central to introducing new hybrids (e.g., California Nursery Company introducing Luther Burbank creations).
